pos: n. (a mere cutting; Paul's contemptuous name for the circumcision party)
etymology: From Latin concidere, to cut in pieces. Paul's Greek is katatome, a mutilation, set against peritome, circumcision. The two words differ by a syllable and by everything: one is a covenant sign, the other is a wound.
biblical_def: Paul fires three warnings in one breath and reserves the sharpest for the religious: “Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision” (Philippians 3:2). The last word is a deliberate insult built on a pun. The Judaizers called themselves he peritome, the circumcision; Paul calls them he katatome, the cutting-up — the word used of the pagan gashings of 1 Kings 18. Severed from the covenant it signified, the rite is no sign at all; it is only a mutilation. Then he takes the title away from them entirely: “For we are the circumcision, which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh” (Philippians 3:3). The three marks are the definition of the true covenant people. Elsewhere he states the plain arithmetic: “For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love” (Galatians 5:6). And Romans locates the real thing where God always located it: “But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God” (Romans 2:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines concision as a cutting off — and notes the Scripture use in Philippians 3:2, where it denotes the Jews in contempt of their zeal for the rite.
webster_full: CONCISION, n. [L. concisio, from concido, to cut off.] A cutting off. In Scripture, the Jews, or those who adhered to circumcision, which was no longer a seal of the covenant.
CONCISE, a. [L. concisus, cut off, brief.] Brief; short, applied to language or style; containing few words.
CIRCUMCISION, n. The act of cutting off the prepuce or foreskin; a ceremony in the Jewish and Mohammedan religions.
MUTILATE, v.t. [L. mutilo.] To cut off a limb or essential part; to maim; to deprive of a material part.
SEAL, n. That which confirms, ratifies or makes stable; assurance; pledge.
scriptures: Philippians 3:2
Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision.
Philippians 3:3
For we are the circumcision, which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh.
Galatians 5:6
For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love.
Romans 2:29
But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God.
corruption_summary: The verse is either softened into a general caution against legalism or hardened into contempt for Israel, when Paul is making a precise claim about who the covenant people now are.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul is a Jew writing about Jewish Christians who required a Jewish rite of Gentile converts, and the argument is intramural in the way Isaiah's and Jeremiah's were. It is not a slur on a people. Romans 2:29 shows the whole ground of the case: the true Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart — which is Moses' own language in Deuteronomy 30:6, not a Christian innovation. Reading Philippians 3:2 as contempt for Israel reverses the apostle who wrote that he could wish himself accursed for his kinsmen.

The commoner corruption in a Reformed congregation is to hear concision and feel safe, because no one here is demanding circumcision. Paul's three marks in verse 3 are the test, and the third is the one that bites: no confidence in the flesh. Flesh here is not appetite but credential — Paul goes on to list his tribe, his sect, his zeal, his blamelessness, and to call the lot of it loss. A church that quietly ranks its members by pedigree, by the sharpness of their doctrine, or by the length of their record has confidence in the flesh, and the rite has changed while the machine has not.
roots_summary: Greek katatome (G2699), a cutting up, mutilation; peritome (G4061), circumcision; sarx (G4561), flesh.
roots_lines: Greek katatome (G2699) — a mutilation; only at Philippians 3:2, a pun against peritome.
Greek peritome (G4061) — circumcision; the title Paul claims for the church in verse 3.
Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh; here the whole register of religious credential.
Hebrew muwl (H4135) — to circumcise; Deuteronomy 30:6, of the heart, long before Paul.
Hebrew gadad (H1413) — to cut oneself; 1 Kings 18:28, the pagan gashing Paul's word evokes.
usage: “Beware of the concision” — a rite cut loose from its covenant is a wound.
“We are the circumcision” — the title reassigned, not abolished.
“No confidence in the flesh” — the mark that still tests a sound church.

pos: n. (the bearing of children; the sphere in which Paul says the woman shall be saved)
etymology: From child + bearing. Paul's Greek is teknogonia, from teknon, child, and gennao, to beget or bear. The definite article in the Greek (tes teknogonias) has long persuaded many that a particular childbearing is in view.
biblical_def: Paul closes his instruction about order in the assembly with a promise: “Notwithstanding she shall be saved in childbearing, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety” (1 Timothy 2:15). He has just grounded that order not in culture but in creation and in the fall: “For Adam was first formed, then Eve” (1 Timothy 2:13), and “And Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression” (1 Timothy 2:14). Verse 15 is the word of hope after verse 14's hard sentence, and it looks straight back to Eden, where the curse fell on the woman precisely at this point and where the promise was given in the same breath — the seed of the woman who should bruise the serpent's head. Reformed readers have taken the verse two principal ways, and both are within the confession: that the woman is preserved through the bearing of children, the very place of her curse becoming the place of her deliverance; or that she is saved through the Childbearing, the birth of Christ from a woman. On either reading the verse is not a wage paid for motherhood. The condition Paul attaches — faith, charity, holiness, sobriety — is the same condition under which any soul is saved, and it is stated in the plural, of women as a body.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives childbearing as the act of producing or bringing forth children; parturition.
webster_full: CHILDBEARING, n. The act of producing or bringing forth children; parturition.
CHILDBIRTH, n. The act of bringing forth a child; travail; labor.
SOBRIETY, n. [L. sobrietas.] Habitual soberness or temperance; freedom from inordinate passion; calmness; seriousness.
TRANSGRESSION, n. The act of passing over or beyond any law or rule of moral duty; the violation of a law or known principle of rectitude; breach of command.
SEED, n. The substance, animal or vegetable, which nature prepares for the reproduction and conservation of the species; offspring; progeny.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 2:15
Notwithstanding she shall be saved in childbearing, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety.
1 Timothy 2:13
For Adam was first formed, then Eve.
1 Timothy 2:14
And Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression.
Galatians 5:6
For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love.
corruption_summary: The verse is read as making motherhood a means of justification, or dismissed with verses 13 and 14 as a cultural remark Paul would not make today.
corruption_paragraphs: The first error turns a promise into a wage, and it wounds the women it means to honour. If salvation came through bearing children, the barren woman, the unmarried woman, and the widow past childbearing would be outside the gospel, and the apostle who wrote Galatians 5:6 — that faith which worketh by love is the whole of it — cannot mean that. Whichever reading of verse 15 is taken, the salvation is Christ's and the condition is faith. Scripture honours Hannah in her barrenness, Anna in her widowhood, and the daughters of Philip who had no husbands.

The second error is the one this dictionary meets more often. Paul grounds his instruction in 1 Timothy 2:13 on the order of creation — Adam first formed, then Eve — and in verse 14 on the manner of the fall, and neither is a fact about first-century Ephesus. An argument from Genesis cannot be retired by a change in the calendar. The complementarian position holds both halves: the order is creational and permanent, and verse 15 is the word of honour and hope that Paul deliberately sets at the end of it, in the place where the curse fell hardest.
roots_summary: Greek teknogonia (G5042), childbearing; sophrosune (G4997), sobriety, soundness of mind; Hebrew zera (H2233), seed.
roots_lines: Greek teknogonia (G5042) — childbearing; only at 1 Timothy 2:15, and articular in the Greek.
Greek sophrosune (G4997) — sound-mindedness, sobriety; the last of the four conditions.
Greek apatao (G538) — to deceive; 1 Timothy 2:14, the woman being deceived.
Greek plasso (G4111) — to form, mould; verse 13, Adam first formed.
Hebrew zera (H2233) — seed; Genesis 3:15, the seed of the woman promised at the curse.
usage: “She shall be saved in childbearing” — a promise set where the curse fell.
“Adam was first formed, then Eve” — the ground is creation, not custom.
“If they continue in faith” — the same condition as any soul's.

pos: n. (the assent and trust of the heart; the instrument by which salvation is received)
etymology: From Old English geleafa, related to lief, dear — belief is what a man holds dear enough to rest on. The KJV uses the noun once, at 2 Thessalonians 2:13, rendering Greek pistis, elsewhere and usually translated faith.
biblical_def: Paul sets belief inside a chain that begins before the world: “But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth” (2 Thessalonians 2:13). Election is the source, the Spirit's sanctifying work is the means, and belief of the truth is the instrument — and the truth is an object, not a mood; a man believes something. Belief is therefore never a work a sinner performs to earn the choosing; it is the appointed way the chosen receive what was given. Its beginnings can be very small and very honest: “And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief” (Mark 9:24) — and Christ healed the boy. Yet the thing itself is indispensable: “But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him” (Hebrews 11:6). And its origin is outside the believer: “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). Belief is not the cause of the new birth but its first breath.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines belief as a persuasion of the truth, or an assent of mind to the truth of a declaration — and in theology, faith, or a firm persuasion of the truths of religion.
webster_full: BELIEF, n. A persuasion of the truth, or an assent of mind to the truth of a declaration, proposition or alleged fact, on the ground of evidence.
BELIEF, n. In theology, faith, or a firm persuasion of the truths of religion.
BELIEF, n. The thing believed; the object of belief; as, the creed contains the belief of the church.
BELIEVE, v.t. To credit upon the authority or testimony of another; to expect or hope with confidence; to trust.
UNBELIEF, n. Incredulity; the withholding of belief. In theology, disbelief of the truth of the gospel.
scriptures: 2 Thessalonians 2:13

But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth:
Mark 9:24
And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
Hebrews 11:6
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
Romans 10:17
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
corruption_summary: Belief is emptied of content and reduced to a posture — believing in oneself, or believing in believing — so that a word with an object becomes a word with none.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage has made belief intransitive. A man is told to believe, and nothing follows the verb; the recommended object is his own capacity or the goodness of the universe. Paul writes belief of the truth, with a genitive that will not come off. Hebrews 11:6 specifies two propositions the comer must hold — that God is, and that He rewards those who seek Him. A belief with no content is not weak faith; it is a different thing wearing the word.

Romans 10:17 closes the other exit. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God, which makes belief a response to something said from outside the man. It cannot be worked up in a meeting by intensity, nor manufactured by deciding hard enough. This is also the comfort of the doctrine. Mark 9:24 is the honest confession of a man whose faith was mixed with its opposite, said with tears, and the Lord did not send him away to acquire a better grade of it first.
roots_summary: Greek pistis (G4102), faith, belief; pisteuo (G4100), to believe, trust; apistia (G570), unbelief; aletheia (G225), truth.
roots_lines: Greek pistis (G4102) — faith; rendered belief at 2 Thessalonians 2:13, faith elsewhere.
Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, to entrust oneself to; the verb of John 3:16.
Greek apistia (G570) — unbelief; Mark 9:24, what the father confessed alongside his faith.
Greek aletheia (G225) — truth; the object belief must have to be belief.
Greek hagiasmos (G38) — sanctification; the Spirit's work named with belief in the same clause.
usage: “Belief of the truth” — a genitive that will not come off.
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief” — honest, mixed, and accepted.
“Faith cometh by hearing” — from outside the man, never worked up within him.

pos: adj. (without end; used of Christ's life and priesthood, and of the genealogies that go nowhere)
etymology: From end + -less. The KJV uses it for two different Greek words: akatalutos, indissoluble, of Christ's life; and aperantos, without limit, of the fables Timothy is to refuse. The same English word covers a glory and a futility.
biblical_def: Hebrews grounds the superiority of Christ's priesthood in the kind of life He has: “Who is made, not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life” (Hebrews 7:16). The Greek is akatalutos — not merely long, but indissoluble, incapable of being broken up. Aaron's sons died and were replaced; this Priest cannot be. The consequence follows at once: “But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood” (Hebrews 7:24), and then the pastoral conclusion the whole argument exists for: “Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). A believer's security rests on the fact that his Advocate does not have a term of office. The same English word carries the opposite weight elsewhere: “Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: so do” (1 Timothy 1:4). There is an endlessness that is life and an endlessness that is only a corridor — a study that never arrives, questions that breed questions, and no edifying at the end of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines endless as without end; having no end or conclusion; perpetual; interminable; and also, incessant, continual.
webster_full: ENDLESS, a. Without end; having no end or conclusion; applied to length, and to duration; as an endless line; endless progression; endless duration; endless bliss.
ENDLESS, a. Perpetual; incessant; continual; as endless praise; endless clamor.
ENDLESSLY, adv. Without end or termination; incessantly; perpetually.
INDISSOLUBLE, a. [L. indissolubilis.] That cannot be dissolved, melted or liquefied; not to be broken or rightfully violated; perpetually binding.
GENEALOGY, n. [Gr.] An account or history of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor; enumeration of ancestors in order of succession.
scriptures: Hebrews 7:16
Who is made, not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life.
Hebrews 7:24
But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood.
Hebrews 7:25
Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
1 Timothy 1:4
Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: so do.
corruption_summary: Endlessness is taken as a bare quantity of time, so that an endless life is heard as a very long one and an endless punishment as an argument against God's love.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 7:16 does not say Christ's life is lengthy; it says it is akatalutos, unable to be dissolved. The difference is the difference between a long lease and a freehold. This is why verse 25 can promise salvation to the uttermost: the intercession does not lapse because the Intercessor cannot lapse. A believer who conceives of eternal life as duration rather than as an indissoluble life shared with Christ has the arithmetic and not the security.

The same category error drives the modern rejection of eternal punishment. Annihilationism and universalism both argue that endless suffering is disproportionate, treating the sentence as a quantity of time set against a quantity of offence. Scripture uses one word, aionios, for the life of the redeemed and the punishment of the lost in a single verse, Matthew 25:46, and the 1689 confesses both. An argument that shortens the one has shortened the other, and the same reasoning that says God's love would not permit an unending punishment has quietly made God's love the judge of God's justice.
roots_summary: Greek akatalutos (G179), indissoluble; aperantos (G562), without limit; aparabatos (G531), unchangeable, untransferable; aionios (G166), eternal.
roots_lines: Greek akatalutos (G179) — that cannot be dissolved; Hebrews 7:16, the power of an endless life.
Greek aperantos (G562) — unlimited, interminable; 1 Timothy 1:4, the genealogies that go nowhere.
Greek aparabatos (G531) — not passing to a successor; Hebrews 7:24, the unchangeable priesthood.
Greek panteles (G3838) — to the uttermost, completely; Hebrews 7:25.
Greek aionios (G166) — eternal; Matthew 25:46, one word over both the life and the punishment.
usage: “The power of an endless life” — indissoluble, not merely long.
“He ever liveth to make intercession” — the Advocate has no term of office.
“Endless genealogies, which minister questions” — a study that never arrives.

pos: n. (a sanctuary held by a king; Amaziah's name for the shrine at Bethel)
etymology: From Late Latin cappella, the shrine housing St Martin's cloak. The KJV uses it once, at Amos 7:13, for Hebrew miqdash melek — the king's sanctuary. The translators' word carries exactly the sense: a holy place that belongs to a man.
biblical_def: Amaziah the priest of Bethel tries to expel Amos with an argument about ownership: “But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court” (Amos 7:13). Every word of it is true and it proves the opposite of what he intends. Bethel was the king's — Jeroboam had made it: “Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt” (1 Kings 12:28). A sanctuary that belongs to a king is a sanctuary God did not command, and the whole indictment of the northern kingdom follows from it. Amos answers by denying that he holds any office Amaziah can revoke: “Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit” (Amos 7:14); and by naming the only commission that matters: “And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel” (Amos 7:15). A herdman with a word from God outranks a priest with a royal chapel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chapel as a house for public worship; a private oratory; or a place of worship subordinate to a church — and gives the origin in the cappella that housed St Martin's cloak.
webster_full: CHAPEL, n. A house for public worship; appropriately, a house for public worship subordinate to a church.
CHAPEL, n. A chapel of ease is a chapel built for the accommodation of a parish, in addition to the principal church.
CHAPEL, n. A private oratory, or place of worship in a palace or great house.
SANCTUARY, n. [L. sanctuarium, from sanctus, sacred.] A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple, called the Holy of Holies.
ORATORY, n. A place destined for prayer; a closet or chapel for private devotions.
scriptures: Amos 7:13
But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court.
1 Kings 12:28

Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.
Amos 7:14
Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit:
Amos 7:15
And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.
corruption_summary: A house of worship becomes a possession — a king's, a donor's, a founder's — and the owner then claims the right to decide what may be preached in it.
corruption_paragraphs: Amaziah's sentence is the permanent temptation of institutional religion, and it does not require a monarchy. Wherever a pulpit is owned — by the family that built the building, by the giver who underwrites the budget, by a board that treats the preacher as staff — the argument from Amos 7:13 is available and will be used. Note that Amaziah does not say Amos is wrong. He says Amos is out of bounds, which is a cheaper and far more effective objection, and one that never has to engage a text.

Jeroboam's calves show the root. He built a convenient sanctuary for a plausible reason — Jerusalem was far, and the journey was a burden — and 1 Kings 12:28 records the pitch in his own words. Worship shaped to what the people will find manageable is the beginning of the king's chapel, and the regulative principle exists to close that door: in corporate worship, what God has commanded is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted. Amos 7:14 is the answer of a free church to an owned one. The herdman held no office Amaziah could take away.
roots_summary: Hebrew miqdash (H4720), sanctuary, holy place; melek (H4428), king; bayith mamlakah (H1004 + H4467), a royal house, the king's court.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqdash (H4720) — a sanctuary; Amos 7:13, rendered chapel because it is the king's.
Hebrew melek (H4428) — king; the possessive that damns the shrine.
Hebrew Beth-el (H1008) — house of God; the name Jacob gave it, kept over a calf.
Hebrew noqed (H5349) — a sheep-breeder, herdman; Amos's trade, Amos 1:1 and 7:14.
Hebrew laqach (H3947) — to take; Amos 7:15, the LORD took me as I followed the flock.
usage: “It is the king's chapel” — true, and the whole indictment.
“It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem” — convenience, offered as mercy.
“The LORD took me as I followed the flock” — the only commission that cannot be revoked.

pos: n. (one who gives orders; a messianic title in Isaiah's great invitation)
etymology: From Latin commendare, to entrust, and mandare, to command. Isaiah 55:4 renders Hebrew metsavveh, one who gives charge — the participle of the verb behind mitzvah, commandment.
biblical_def: Isaiah's open invitation is not to a philosophy but to a Person with authority: “Behold, I have given him for a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people” (Isaiah 55:4). Three titles in one line, and the third is military. He testifies, He goes in front, and He gives orders. The chapter has already set the terms of the covenant He heads: “Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David” (Isaiah 55:3) — a covenant whose mercies are sure because they rest on David's greater Son and not on the comers. And the invitation itself is free to the penniless: “Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1). Isaiah had already named the child on whose shoulder the government would rest: “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6). Grace is free, and the One who gives it is a Commander. Both stand in the same chapter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a commander as a chief; one who has supreme authority; a leader; the chief officer of an army, or of any division of it.
webster_full: COMMANDER, n. A chief; one who has supreme authority; a leader; the chief officer of an army, or of any division of it.
COMMANDER, n. One who has supreme authority over a ship or fleet; a commanding officer.
COMMAND, v.t. [L. mando, to command, to commit.] To bid; to order; to direct; to charge; implying authority, and power to control, and to require obedience.
LEADER, n. One that leads or conducts; a guide; a conductor; a chief; a commander.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event. That which furnishes evidence or proof.
scriptures: Isaiah 55:4
Behold, I have given him for a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people.
Isaiah 55:3
Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David.
Isaiah 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
Isaiah 9:6

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
corruption_summary: The invitation of Isaiah 55 is preached without verse 4, so that Christ is offered as a Saviour to be received and not as a Commander to be obeyed.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 55:1 is one of the freest offers in Scripture — no money, no price, come and buy. Three verses later the same chapter names the One offered as a leader and commander. The gospel that keeps verse 1 and drops verse 4 produces a convert who has received a benefit and acknowledged no authority, and Scripture knows no such creature. The 1689 confesses that saving faith receives Christ as prophet, priest, and king; a faith that takes the priest and declines the king has divided a Person who cannot be divided.

The opposite error deserves naming in the same breath, because the remedy for cheap grace is not a price tag. Verse 1 is addressed to the man who hath no money, and every attempt to add a qualification — sufficient sorrow, a settled life, a demonstrated seriousness — contradicts the verse it claims to guard. The mercies are called sure in verse 3 precisely because they do not rest on the comer. Free to enter, and a Commander inside: that is the whole chapter, and neither half may be preached alone.
roots_summary: Hebrew metsavveh (H6680), one commanding, from tsavah, to give charge; nagid (H5057), leader, prince; ed (H5707), a witness.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsavah (H6680) — to lay charge upon, command; its participle gives commander.
Hebrew nagid (H5057) — leader, prince, one set in front; the second title of Isaiah 55:4.
Hebrew ed (H5707) — a witness; the first title, one who testifies.
Hebrew chesed Dawid ha-neemanim (H2617) — the sure mercies of David; quoted in Acts 13:34.
Hebrew misrah (H4951) — government, rule; Isaiah 9:6, upon his shoulder.
usage: “A leader and commander to the people” — three titles, and one gives orders.
“He that hath no money” — the qualification is that there is none.
“The sure mercies of David” — sure because they do not rest on the comer.

pos: n. (a settlement of Roman citizens abroad; the civic status of Philippi)
etymology: From Latin colonia, a settlement, from colere, to cultivate. Luke's Greek keeps the Latin as a loan-word, kolonia, because the thing was Roman: a transplanted piece of Rome, governed by Roman law, whose people held Roman citizenship on foreign soil.
biblical_def: Luke records a civic detail that Paul will later preach from: “And from thence to Philippi, which is the chief city of that part of Macedonia, and a colony: and we were in that city abiding certain days” (Acts 16:12). A Roman colony was not a trading post but a transplanted Rome — Roman law, Roman magistrates, Roman citizenship held by men who had never seen the city they belonged to. The status becomes a lever in the same chapter: “But Paul said unto them, They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast us into prison; and now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us out” (Acts 16:37). And the first convert in Europe is won there by a sovereign work with no leverage in it at all: “And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul” (Acts 16:14). Writing back to that church years later, Paul uses the civic word they knew best: “For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20). The Greek behind conversation is politeuma, commonwealth — the register of citizens. Philippi understood exactly what he meant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colony as a company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country, and remaining subject to the jurisdiction of the parent state.
webster_full: COLONY, n. [L. colonia, from colo, to cultivate, to inhabit.] A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country to cultivate and inhabit it, and remaining subject to the jurisdiction of the parent state.
COLONY, n. The country planted or colonized; a plantation.
COLONY, n. A collection of animals; as a colony of ants.
CITIZEN, n. The native of a city, or an inhabitant who enjoys the freedom and privileges of the city in which he resides.
COMMONWEALTH, n. An established form of government, or civil polity; the whole body of people in a state.
scriptures: Acts 16:12
And from thence to Philippi, which is the chief city of that part of Macedonia, and a colony: and we were in that city abiding certain days.
Acts 16:37

But Paul said unto them, They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast us into prison; and now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us out.
Acts 16:14
And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
Philippians 3:20
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: Heavenly citizenship is read as detachment from the present world, when a colony is precisely a body that lives under its home law in a foreign place.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misreading is devotional. Our conversation is in heaven gets taken to mean that earth is a waiting room, and the Christian's business here is merely to endure until the transfer. A colony is the exact opposite of that. Philippi did not sit loose to Macedonia; it planted Roman law in Macedonian soil and held it there. The principle to recover is that heavenly citizenship is a claim on how a Christian lives on this street, not a reason to disengage from it.

Acts 16 shows both halves in one chapter. Paul uses his Roman citizenship without embarrassment to demand lawful treatment from magistrates who had beaten him uncondemned — a Christian may hold a civil authority to its own law. And the actual conversion in verse 14 owes nothing to status or leverage: the Lord opened Lydia's heart. The colony holds its rights in the city and gets its citizens by sovereign grace, and confusing which is which has ruined a good deal of Christian political thinking in both directions.
roots_summary: Greek kolonia (G2862), a Roman colony; politeuma (G4175), commonwealth, citizenship; Rhomaios (G4514), a Roman.
roots_lines: Greek kolonia (G2862) — a colony; a Latin loan-word, only at Acts 16:12.
Greek politeuma (G4175) — commonwealth, register of citizens; Philippians 3:20, rendered conversation.
Greek politeuomai (G4176) — to live as a citizen; Philippians 1:27, the verb of the same root.
Greek Rhomaios (G4514) — a Roman; Acts 16:37, the status Paul invokes.
Greek dianoigo (G1272) — to open thoroughly; Acts 16:14, whose heart the Lord opened.
usage: “Philippi…and a colony” — a transplanted Rome under Roman law.
“Being Romans” — a citizen may hold a magistrate to his own law.
“Our conversation is in heaven” — the register a Christian's name is kept in.

pos: n. (one who uncovers what is hidden; a divine title confessed by Nebuchadnezzar)
etymology: From Latin revelare, to draw back the veil, from velum, a veil. Daniel 2:47 renders the Aramaic participle of gelah, to uncover, in Nebuchadnezzar's own confession — a pagan king's title for the God of Israel.
biblical_def: Nebuchadnezzar has demanded the impossible — the dream and its interpretation — and the wise men of Babylon have told him no man on earth can do it. When Daniel does, the king confesses more than he knows: “The king answered unto Daniel, and said, Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret” (Daniel 2:47). Daniel had already refused the credit and set the title where it belonged: “But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these” (Daniel 2:28). The ground of it is what God is in Himself: “He revealeth the deep and secret things: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him” (Daniel 2:22). Darkness hides nothing from Him because the light is where He lives. And the settled pattern of His self-disclosure is through His appointed servants: “Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7). Revelation is not something men extract. It is something God gives, and He gives it through a word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a revealer as one who discloses or makes known; one who discovers to the view what was before hidden or unknown.
webster_full: REVEALER, n. One that discloses or makes known; that which shows or makes known.
REVEAL, v.t. [L. revelo; re and velo, to veil.] To disclose; to discover; to show; to make known something before unknown or concealed.
REVEAL, v.t. To disclose, discover or make known from heaven. God has been pleased to reveal his will to man.

REVELATION, n. The act of disclosing or discovering to others what was before unknown to them. In theology, the disclosure or communication of truth to men by God himself, or by his authorized agents.
SECRET, n. Something studiously concealed; a thing kept from general knowledge.
scriptures: Daniel 2:47
The king answered unto Daniel, and said, Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret.
Daniel 2:28
But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these;
Daniel 2:22
He revealeth the deep and secret things: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him.
Amos 3:7
Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.
corruption_summary: Revelation is treated as an ongoing private supply — impressions, words, downloads — rather than as the closed and sufficient Scripture God has given.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 2 is the favourite chapter of every movement that claims fresh revelation, and it argues against them. Daniel receives the secret, and the secret is immediately public, verifiable, and about God's kingdom rather than Daniel's life — he does not get a private word for his own guidance. The New Apostolic Reformation, the prophetic conference circuit, and the personal-word culture that trickles down from them all invert this. Where the modern claim cannot be tested, Deuteronomy 18 has already given the test and the penalty for failing it.

The dictionary is cessationist with the Reformed mainstream, and the positive ground is the better argument. Hebrews opens by saying God spoke in time past by the prophets and has in these last days spoken by His Son, which is a completion and not a pause. The 1689 confesses that those former ways of revealing His will are now ceased, and that Scripture is therefore most necessary and sufficient. God is still the revealer of secrets, as Daniel 2:22 says He is by nature. What He has revealed, He has put in a book, and the sufficiency of that book is the comfort of the ordinary Christian who has no dream to report.
roots_summary: Aramaic gelah (H1541), to uncover, reveal; Hebrew galah (H1540), to uncover; sod (H5475), a secret counsel; Greek apokalupto (G601), to unveil.
roots_lines: Aramaic gelah (H1541) — to reveal, uncover; the participle behind revealer of secrets.
Aramaic raz (H7328) — a mystery, secret; the word for what the king demanded.
Hebrew sod (H5475) — intimate counsel; Amos 3:7, the secret told to His servants.
Hebrew nabi (H5030) — a prophet; the appointed channel, not the source.
Greek apokalupsis (G602) — an unveiling; the New Testament word for the same act.
usage: “A revealer of secrets” — confessed by a pagan king.
“The light dwelleth with him” — darkness hides nothing from where He lives.
“He revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets” — given through a word, not extracted.

pos: n. pl. (those who approach; the worshippers the old sacrifices could not perfect)
etymology: From come + -er. Hebrews 10:1 renders the Greek participle tous proserchomenous, those coming to — a word of approach used throughout the epistle for drawing near to God. The KJV's plain noun keeps the motion in it.
biblical_def: Hebrews states the limit of the whole levitical system in one sentence: “For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect” (Hebrews 10:1). Note who is being described. Not the careless, but the comers — the devout who came, year by year, exactly as commanded. The system was not failing them through their negligence; it was designed as a shadow, and a shadow cannot perfect anybody. The contrast lands in the same chapter: “For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14) — one offering, not repeated; perfected for ever, not annually renewed. The epistle draws the same line earlier: “For the law made nothing perfect, but the bringing in of a better hope did; by the which we draw nigh unto God” (Hebrews 7:19). And the conclusion is an invitation to approach with a confidence the old comers never had: “Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a comer as one that comes; one who approaches; one that is present or has arrived.
webster_full: COMER, n. One that comes; one that approaches; one that has arrived and is present.
COME, v.i. [Sax. cuman.] To move towards; to advance nearer, in any manner, and from any distance.
PERFECT, v.t. [L. perficio, to complete.] To finish or complete, so as to leave nothing wanting; to give to any thing all that is requisite to its nature and kind.
SHADOW, n. In Scripture, a type; that which represents something else; an imperfect and faint representation.
APPROACH, v.i. To come or go near, in place; to draw near; to advance nearer.
scriptures: Hebrews 10:1

For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.
Hebrews 10:14
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
Hebrews 7:19
For the law made nothing perfect, but the bringing in of a better hope did; by the which we draw nigh unto God.
Hebrews 10:22
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
corruption_summary: Hebrews 10:1 is taken as a verdict on the piety of Old Testament worshippers, when it is a verdict on what a shadow is able to do.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter is sometimes preached as though the Israelites who brought their lambs were the dull and legalistic foil to the New Testament believer. They were the comers. They obeyed a command God had given, at the place He appointed, in the manner He prescribed, and Hebrews 11 fills a chapter with their names as men and women of faith. The limitation was built into the shadow by God's own design, so that the repetition itself — year by year continually — would preach the insufficiency and teach a nation to look for something else.

The verse also stands against every system that reinstalls repetition. Where a sacrifice is offered again, whatever it is called, Hebrews 10:14 is contradicted in its plainest word: one offering, and perfected for ever. The Roman mass is the historic case the Reformation named. But a low-church congregation can build the same treadmill out of rededications, annual recommitments, and an altar call that must be answered afresh each time assurance dims. Verse 22 tells the comer to draw near in full assurance, which is the one posture a treadmill can never produce.
roots_summary: Greek proserchomai (G4334), to come to, approach; teleioo (G5048), to perfect, complete; skia (G4639), a shadow; plerophoria (G4136), full assurance.
roots_lines: Greek proserchomai (G4334) — to draw near; its participle is the comers of Hebrews 10:1.
Greek skia (G4639) — a shadow; set against eikon, the very image, in the same verse.
Greek teleioo (G5048) — to bring to completion; what the law could not do and one offering did.
Greek eis to dienekes (G1336) — for ever, continuously; Hebrews 10:14, the perfecting that does not lapse.
Greek plerophoria (G4136) — full assurance; the posture commanded in Hebrews 10:22.
usage: “The comers thereunto” — the devout, not the careless.
“Year by year continually” — the repetition was itself the sermon.
“Perfected for ever them that are sanctified” — one offering, not renewed.

pos: n. (the summing up; the Preacher's final verdict on the whole matter)
etymology: From Latin concludere, to shut up together, from claudere, to close. Ecclesiastes 12:13 renders Hebrew soph dabar — the end of the word, the last thing to be said after everything else has been said and found empty.
biblical_def: Ecclesiastes has walked a man through wisdom, pleasure, labour, wealth, and death, and returned the same verdict on each: “Vanity of vanities, saith the preacher; all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 12:8), which is where the book began — “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Then the Preacher stops arguing and sums: “Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man” (Ecclesiastes 12:13). Two imperatives, one inward and one outward, and the Hebrew literally says this is the whole of man — not a duty among his duties but the sum of what he is for. The reason follows immediately, and it is the reason nothing under the sun was ever really vain: “For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil” (Ecclesiastes 12:14). A judgment that reaches every secret thing is what makes a hidden life matter. The book's practical counsel is set one page earlier, aimed at the young, who think they have time to reach the conclusion later: “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them” (Ecclesiastes 12:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conclusion as the end, close, or termination; the final result; and, in logic, the inference which follows from the premises.
webster_full: CONCLUSION, n. [L. conclusio.] End; close; the last part. The end, issue or event of an experiment or trial.
CONCLUSION, n. In logic, the inference or proposition which follows from two or more premises in an argument.
CONCLUSION, n. Final determination; final judgment or decision.
CONCLUDE, v.t. [L. concludo; con and claudo, to shut.] To shut; to close. To end; to finish. To determine; to decide.
VANITY, n. [L. vanitas.] Emptiness; want of substance to satisfy desire; uncertainty; inanity.
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 12:13
Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
Ecclesiastes 12:8
Vanity of vanities, saith the preacher; all is vanity.
Ecclesiastes 12:14
For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil.
Ecclesiastes 12:1
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
corruption_summary: Ecclesiastes is read as an ancient statement of absurdity with a pious ending bolted on, so the book's own conclusion is treated as the one part that does not belong.
corruption_paragraphs: The existentialist reading takes the vanity and discards the verdict, and it has to argue that 12:13 was added by a later hand to tame the book. Nothing in the text supports the surgery. The Preacher's method throughout is to test a thing to destruction and report the result, and the conclusion is the report — the only item that survived the testing. A book that ends with judgment on every secret thing is not a monument to meaninglessness. It is the argument that meaning is not found under the sun because it was never located there.

The church's own version of the error is to use 12:13 as a lid. The conclusion is quoted, the eleven chapters of honest complaint are skipped, and a believer in genuine darkness learns that his questions are unwelcome. God gave the whole book, complaint included, and gave it to a covenant people. Fear God and keep his commandments is where the Preacher arrives after the questioning, not a substitute for it, and a congregation that will not walk the road with a man cannot hand him the destination.

roots_lines: Hebrew soph (H5490) — end, conclusion; soph dabar, the end of the word or matter.
Hebrew hebel (H1892) — a breath, vapour; the vanity repeated thirty-eight times in the book.
Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear, revere; the first of the two imperatives.
Hebrew kol ha-adam (H3605 + H120) — the whole of man; rendered the whole duty of man.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment; Ecclesiastes 12:14, reaching every secret thing.
usage: “Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter” — after everything else was tested.
“This is the whole duty of man” — literally, the whole of man.
“Every secret thing” — what makes a hidden life matter.
